senses.gloss: To cause a particular feeling in people, especially confidence or fear.
examples: His calm voice *inspires* confidence.
The announcement *inspired* very little trust on Wall Street.
Her steady hands have *inspired* confidence in every patient she treats.

senses.gloss: To be the thing that gives someone the idea for a work or a plan.
senses.ru: вдохновлять, вдохновить (послужить источником); навести на мысль
examples: A trip to Peru *inspired* her first cookbook.
The film was *inspired* by events in a small Ohio town.
Nobody knows what *inspires* his strangest songs.

senses.gloss: To place someone formally in an important position or office.
senses.ru: вводить в должность, ввести; назначать, назначить (на пост)
examples: The board *installed* a new chief executive in March.
She was *installed* as dean last fall.
They are *installing* their own people at every level of the agency.

senses.gloss: To teach a subject or a skill to someone.
examples: She *instructs* beginners in the pool on Saturday mornings.
A retired pilot *instructed* our ground school class.
He has been *instructing* teenagers in woodworking for twenty years.

senses.gloss: To protect someone from something unpleasant that other people have to face.
examples: Tenure *insulates* professors from that kind of pressure.
Their savings *insulated* the family from the worst of the layoffs.
No company is completely *insulated* from a recession.

senses.gloss: To stop something for a while before it is finished.
examples: Rain *interrupted* the game in the fourth inning.
Nothing is allowed to *interrupt* the broadcast.
Service has been *interrupted* twice this week.

senses.gloss: To bring something into use for the first time, such as a product, a rule, or a bill.
examples: The company *introduced* its first electric truck last year.
Two senators plan to *introduce* the bill in January.
Seat belts were *introduced* in American cars in the 1950s.

senses.gloss: To give someone their first experience of something.
examples: My uncle *introduced* me to jazz when I was nine.
The course *introduces* students to basic statistics.
He had never been *introduced* to real Mexican food before that trip.

senses.gloss: To intrude on something private, especially a person's privacy.
examples: The photographers *invaded* her privacy at the hospital.
Reading someone's texts *invades* their privacy.
He has never *invaded* his kids' privacy that way.

senses.gloss: To make an unwanted reaction more likely.
examples: Comments like that *invite* criticism.
The vague wording *invited* a lawsuit.
By ignoring the warnings, they were *inviting* disaster.

senses.gloss: To separate one thing from everything around it so that it can be examined or dealt with on its own.
examples: Engineers are trying to *isolate* the cause of the failure.
The lab *isolated* the virus within a week.
Once we had *isolated* the bad cable, the network came back up.

senses.gloss: To push something pointed into or toward something.
examples: He *jabbed* a finger at the map.
Don't *jab* the fork into the meat like that.
The nurse was *jabbing* at his arm, looking for a vein.

senses.gloss: To force something into a space that is almost too small for it.
examples: She *jammed* three sweaters into her backpack.
Don't *jam* the papers in like that — they'll tear.
He had *jammed* his hands into his pockets against the cold.

senses.gloss: To play music with other people without planning it beforehand.
examples: They *jam* in the garage every Sunday.
We *jammed* for three hours after the show.
The band was still *jamming* when I left.

senses.gloss: To make someone remember something they had forgotten.
examples: Maybe this photo will *jog* your memory.
The smell of chalk *jogged* an old memory.
We're hoping the recording *jogs* his memory.

senses.gloss: To become a member of a group, a club, or an organization.
examples: She *joined* the Navy right after high school.
How much does it cost to *join* the gym?
He has *joined* three different book clubs this year.

senses.gloss: To come and be with someone in what they are doing.
examples: Will you *join* us for dinner?
Two more reporters *joined* them at the table.
Thanks for *joining* us tonight.

senses.gloss: To shock someone suddenly, often into acting.
examples: The news *jolted* the whole company.
It took a failing grade to *jolt* him into studying.
Voters were *jolted* by the sudden resignation.

senses.gloss: To criticize someone's choices or morals, usually unfairly.
examples: Don't *judge* me — you weren't there.
She felt *judged* the moment she walked in.
People were *judging* him for something he said years ago.

senses.gloss: To manage several jobs or responsibilities at the same time.
examples: He *juggles* two jobs and night school.
For years she *juggled* work and three kids.
I'm tired of *juggling* everyone else's schedules.

senses.gloss: To rise suddenly and by a large amount.
senses.ru: резко расти, подскочить, взлететь (о ценах, числах)
examples: Gas prices *jumped* forty cents overnight.
Sales *jump* every December.
Her score has *jumped* almost 200 points.

senses.gloss: To move suddenly because something has startled you.
examples: Sorry, I didn't mean to make you *jump*.
She *jumped* when the door slammed.
He was *jumping* at every little noise.

senses.gloss: To attack someone suddenly, usually in a group (informal).
examples: Three guys *jumped* him outside the bar.
He got *jumped* walking home from work.
Be careful, or somebody will *jump* you for that phone.

senses.gloss: To succeed in stopping a bad habit or an addiction.
examples: He finally *kicked* the habit at fifty.
It took her two years to *kick* her soda habit.
He has *kicked* worse addictions than this one.

senses.gloss: To cause someone a lot of physical pain.
senses.ru: сильно болеть, ныть (о ногах, спине); доставлять сильную боль
examples: My feet are *killing* me.
That hike *killed* my knees.
Cheap headphones *kill* my ears after an hour.

senses.gloss: To stop something from going ahead or from running — a plan, a story, or a machine.
examples: The committee *killed* the bill without a vote.
*Kill* the engine before you open the hood.
The story was *killed* an hour before the paper went to press.

senses.gloss: To hit a door with your hand so that the people inside hear you.
examples: Somebody is *knocking* at the door.
She *knocked* twice and waited.
*Knock* before you come in.

senses.gloss: To criticize someone or something, often unfairly (informal).
examples: Don't *knock* it until you've tried it.
Critics *knocked* the plan as too expensive.
He's always *knocking* somebody else's work.

senses.gloss: To describe someone or something as a particular type, often unfairly.
senses.ru: навешивать ярлык, навесить ярлык; называть, объявлять (кем-л.)
examples: Teachers *labeled* him a troublemaker in third grade.
Don't *label* people you've never met.
Once you have been *labeled* difficult, it follows you.

senses.gloss: To add alcohol or a drug to food or a drink, usually secretly.
examples: Somebody *laced* the punch with vodka.
The pills were *laced* with fentanyl.
He's been *lacing* his coffee with whiskey since noon.

senses.gloss: To fall behind other people or things in progress or development.
examples: US students *lag* behind much of the world in math.
Sales *lagged* all through the spring.
Wages have *lagged* behind prices for a decade.

senses.gloss: To succeed in getting something that many people want.
examples: She *landed* a job at the museum.
How did a first-year firm *land* that contract?
He has *landed* every account he went after.

senses.gloss: To drink by scooping up liquid with the tongue, the way an animal does.
examples: The dog *lapped* water from the bowl.
Kittens *lap* milk instead of sucking it.
The cat was still *lapping* at the puddle.

senses.gloss: To tie something firmly in place with rope.
examples: They *lashed* the kayaks to the roof of the car.
*Lash* the boxes down before we hit the highway.
The crew had *lashed* everything to the deck.

senses.gloss: To pass money from crime through legal businesses so that it looks honest.
examples: They *laundered* the cash through a chain of car washes.
It is not easy to *launder* that much money.
He admitted *laundering* more than a million dollars.

senses.gloss: To knock a building or an area completely flat.
senses.ru: сносить, снести; сравнивать с землёй, сровнять
examples: The tornado *leveled* half the town.
Crews will *level* the old high school this summer.
The whole block had been *leveled* years before I was born.

senses.gloss: To aim a criticism or an accusation at someone.
examples: Critics *leveled* the same charge at her last year.
He *levels* his complaints at the coaching staff, not the players.
Serious accusations have been *leveled* against the department.
